analysis.title: Rebalance into fixed income
key_insights: UBS CIO recommends adding to fixed income allocations in 2027, citing reliable portfolio income, diversification of equity risk if growth weakens or financial instability rises, and added income from EM and high yield bonds.

Base case is supportive for bonds. If inflation moderates as UBS expects, yields should decline modestly, giving coupon income plus capital gains. Geopolitical and fiscal uncertainty could keep yields volatile near term.

In the UBS 'AI bust' scenario, weaker capital expenditure and monetary easing lower yields and support bond prices while equities decline. Bonds could also benefit if financial instability prompted policy intervention.
Elevated starting yields give an income cushion that can offset part of the price impact of a moderate rise in yields, especially in short and intermediate maturities.

Preferred maturity range is two to 10 years. Shorter maturities carry less sensitivity to fiscal and term premium risks. Longer maturities within the range diversify more and gain more if yields fall. UBS would extend beyond 10 years only selectively because of heavy expected issuance and fiscal uncertainty.

UBS favors EM and high yield bonds on a relative basis. EM sovereign yields are around 7.1% (JPM EMBI) and EM corporate around 7.0% (JPM CEMBI). US high yield yields around 8.3% (ICE BofA US High Yield index).

EM fundamentals are stronger than in prior cycles: higher FX reserves, better current account positions, manageable fiscal deficits and fewer distressed sovereigns. Investors should focus on external balances, fiscal credibility and political stability.

US high yield: around 60% of the market is rated BB versus about 40% a decade ago. UBS expects defaults to stay near 2%. About 3% of the market matures over the next year. Recent spread widening is concentrated in a small number of capital-intensive or structurally challenged borrowers.

In high yield UBS favors the shorter end of its preferred maturity range and issuers with sustainable cash flows, manageable leverage and limited refinancing needs, and limits exposure to the weakest borrowers.

Risks to the EM and high yield view: a sharp global slowdown, renewed dollar strength, prolonged monetary tightening or wider credit spreads. In an AI-led investment downturn, weaker growth and wider spreads would hurt both markets, particularly high yield.

For CHF investors, Swiss government bond yields have not risen enough to be a compelling standalone income source because Swiss inflation and policy rates are low. High-quality Swiss issuers add some yield without currency risk, but UBS says investors seeking higher cash flow need to look beyond Swiss investment grade credit.
Foreign currency bonds offer higher nominal yields, but currency volatility can overwhelm bond returns, so UBS advises retaining currency exposure selectively.
Swiss dividend-paying equities yield around 3.1% versus a 2.4% average since 2004. Dividends contributed more than half of the SMI's total return over the past three decades.

Selling options or using structured yield strategies can add premium income, but income may be conditional, upside capped and losses significant. UBS favors diversified underlyings, staggered maturities and disciplined position sizing.
